content: A cystocele occurs when the wall between a woman’s bladder and her vagina weakens, allowing the bladder to drop or protrude into the vagina. This condition can lead to discomfort and issues with emptying the bladder. Symptoms of Cystocele When the bladder drops from its normal position, it can cause two primary problems: involuntary urine leakage and incomplete bladder emptying. In some women, the fallen bladder stretches the opening into the urethra, leading to urine leakage during activities that increase pressure on the bladder, such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or physical movement. Causes of Cystocele A cystocele can result from muscle strain during childbirth. Other forms of strain, such as heavy lifting or repeated straining during bowel movements, can also cause the bladder to fall. The hormone estrogen plays a role in maintaining the strength of the muscles around the vagina. After menopause, when estrogen production ceases, the muscles supporting the vagina and bladder may weaken, increasing the risk of cystocele. Cystoceles are classified into three grades: Grade 1 (mild): The bladder droops slightly into the vagina. Grade 2 (moderate): The bladder sinks far enough to reach the vaginal opening. Grade 3 (severe): The bladder bulges out through the vaginal opening. Risk Factors Certain factors increase the likelihood of developing a cystocele: Vaginal childbirth Advancing age, particularly in postmenopausal women Hysterectomy (surgical removal of the uterus) Genetic predisposition to connective tissue disorders When to Seek Medical Attention You should consult a healthcare provider if you experience symptoms associated with a cystocele. Diagnosis A physician can often diagnose a grade 2 or grade 3 cystocele based on symptom descriptions and a physical examination of the vagina, as the protruding bladder may be visible. A voiding cystourethrogram, an X-ray taken during urination, can help visualize the bladder’s shape and identify any obstructions to normal urine flow. Additional tests may be required to evaluate other parts of the urinary system. Treatment Options Treatment depends on the severity of the cystocele: Mild cases: If the cystocele is not bothersome, the doctor may recommend avoiding heavy lifting or straining to prevent worsening of the condition. Moderate cases: A pessary, a device inserted into the vagina to support the bladder, may be recommended. Pessaries come in various shapes and sizes to ensure a comfortable fit. They must be removed and cleaned regularly to prevent infections or ulcers. Severe cases: Surgery may be necessary to reposition and support the bladder. This procedure is typically performed by a gynecologist, urologist, or urogynecologist. The most common surgical approach involves making an incision in the vaginal wall and repairing the area to tighten the tissue layers, providing better support for the bladder. Recovery may require a hospital stay of several days and a full recovery period of 4 to 6 weeks. Possible Complications Recurrent urinary tract infections are a potential complication of cystocele. Prevention Preventive measures for cystocele include: Performing Kegel exercises, especially after childbirth, to strengthen pelvic floor muscles. Consuming a diet rich in fiber and fluids to prevent constipation. Promptly treating conditions like constipation or chronic coughing. Maintaining a healthy weight through a balanced diet and regular exercise.
